claims.text: Under rapid heating and cooling, formation of uniform single-phase noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is kinetically limited by an insufficient atomic-diffusion window.
Insufficient atomic mobility causes phase separation and elemental segregation.
Insufficient atomic mobility causes uncontrolled nanoparticle morphology.
An intermediate isothermal hold can extend the effective atomic-mixing time and permit additional atomic rearrangement.
A hold at 150–200 °C is an appropriate intervention for extending atomic mixing.
Graded precursor-ligand decomposition can delay complete atomic release and extend the atomic-mixing period.
Extending the atomic-mixing time promotes homogeneous nucleation.
Extended atomic mixing favors formation of a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Controlled precursor decomposition minimizes local supersaturation and prevents early nucleation that would otherwise lead to segregation.
Additional time for atomic rearrangement balances rapid nucleation against atomic mobility.
The intervention alleviates kinetic trapping and reduces local concentration gradients.
Relative to continuous rapid heating and cooling, the intervention will produce a more uniform elemental distribution and less elemental clustering or segregation.
Relative to the baseline, the intervention will improve particle morphology.
Moderated reaction kinetics may lower the observed onset temperature for precursor decomposition.
A one-step rapid-heating and rapid-cooling process without a controlled mixing window has a higher likelihood of phase separation, segregation, and poorly controlled morphology.
The mechanism is applicable to rapidly processed noble-metal systems containing at least five elements.
The intervention becomes ineffective when the hold is too short to overcome diffusion barriers.
The intervention becomes less effective if the processing-temperature window is too wide.

contradictions.description: The thermal hold is described as occurring after rapid initial heating, while the proposed mediator and mechanism say that it prevents or eliminates early nucleation. If nucleation already occurs during the initial rapid-heating stage, a subsequent hold cannot prevent those earlier events without an additional timing argument.
